h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Grand Rapids
intro: Grand Rapids is a tight housing market. Inventory is thin, owner-occupant buyers compete hard for move-in-ready homes, and the older houses that investors can still buy at a discount usually carry a long list of deferred repairs. That puts the pressure on estimating. If you guess low on a Creston foursquare or a West Side cottage, the spread disappears quickly. Genstone Construction gives you a written repair number before you commit capital through our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, which prices the work, sets it against the resale or refinance value you are counting on and flags whether the offer still makes sense. After closing, the job runs from an itemized scope that spells out labor, materials and when each draw is due, under one field manager, with vetted and licensed local trades who are used to the city’s rental certification inspections and historic district reviews. You pay nothing upfront, draws follow completed work, and you can follow progress and documentation without driving across town or across the country to check on the job.
housingStock:
The oldest housing in Grand Rapids climbs the hill east of downtown. Heritage Hill holds large Victorian, Italianate, Queen Anne, Prairie and Colonial Revival homes built for the lumber barons, furniture makers and professionals who made the city’s fortune in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Many of them were divided into apartments during the middle of the last century, and some are still multi-unit today. Farther east, Eastown and East Hills fill in with foursquares, Craftsman bungalows and modest Victorians from roughly the 1890s through the 1920s.

North of downtown, Creston and Belknap Lookout contain small frame houses on narrow lots, many of them on slopes that affect drainage and foundation work. Belknap in particular sits on a steep bluff, so access for dumpsters and material deliveries is something to plan for. The West Side, around John Ball Park and Fulton Heights, was a working-class Dutch and Polish area with compact frame homes, and it now attracts students and young workers. On the southeast side, Garfield Park, Baxter and Roosevelt Park hold older frame housing, a substantial share of it rented. Alger Heights and Ottawa Hills are later, with brick Tudors, colonials and bungalows from the 1920s through the 1950s.

For a rehab, expect older basements built of fieldstone, rubble or brick in the pre-1910 houses and concrete block in later ones. Balloon framing is common in the Victorian stock, which matters for fire blocking when walls are opened. Knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains, asbestos pipe wrap and lead paint all show up regularly. Large old houses often have multiple roof layers and complex flashing around dormers and turrets, which raises roofing costs well above a simple gable.

commonIssues.title: Lead hazards in older rentals
commonIssues.body: Lead poisoning in children has been a persistent concern in the older neighborhoods on the southeast and west sides, and Grand Rapids and Kent County have put real effort into reducing it. Peeling paint on window sashes, porches and exterior trim is the usual source. For investors, this means lead-safe work practices on almost every job, careful window decisions and paint stabilization before a rental is occupied. The city’s rental certification inspection will look at deteriorated paint, so plan for it in the scope.

commonIssues.title: Fieldstone and rubble foundations
commonIssues.body: Many pre-1910 Grand Rapids homes sit on fieldstone or rubble foundations with lime mortar that has washed out over the years. Water seeps through, mortar crumbles and loose stones can shift. Repairs range from repointing and parging to installing interior drainage and a sump. When a house is on a slope, as many are in Belknap Lookout and Creston, the uphill wall usually takes the most water. We price foundation work after looking at the walls directly.

commonIssues.title: Converted multi-unit Victorians
commonIssues.body: Large homes in Heritage Hill and Eastown were often divided into several apartments decades ago, sometimes with little regard to fire separation, egress or electrical capacity. When you buy one, you may find undersized services, extension wiring, kitchens added in former bedrooms and stairs that do not meet current code. Bringing such a building up to standard can be a big job, and returning it to single-family use is a separate question with its own zoning and permit path.

commonIssues.title: Ice dams and complex roofs
commonIssues.body: Lake-effect snow off Lake Michigan means Grand Rapids roofs carry heavy snow loads, and poorly insulated attics in older homes create ice dams at the eaves. Water backs up under shingles and stains plaster ceilings and walls. Victorian houses with dormers, valleys and turrets are particularly prone. A good rehab adds attic insulation and air sealing, ice and water shield at the eaves and valleys, and proper ventilation, not just new shingles.

commonIssues.title: Lead and galvanized water lines
commonIssues.body: Older homes in the city may still have lead service lines or galvanized steel lines that were once connected to lead. The City of Grand Rapids has been replacing lead service lines, but the private plumbing inside the house is the owner’s responsibility. If you are renovating a pre-war house, plan to replace galvanized supply piping inside, and check the material of the service line before finishing the basement or replacing the water heater.

investorMarket:
Grand Rapids has drawn steady population and job growth for years, anchored by health care along the Medical Mile, manufacturing and a growing downtown. That has created a competitive market where owner-occupant buyers often outbid investors on clean houses. As a result, investor opportunities tend to be properties that need serious work or carry complications a typical buyer will not accept.

Flips work best in neighborhoods where buyers are willing to pay for renovated older homes, such as Eastown, East Hills, Alger Heights, Ottawa Hills and the better streets of Creston. Buyers there want updated kitchens and baths but also care about original woodwork, built-ins and hardwood floors. On the West Side, near the Grand Valley State University downtown campus, smaller houses can work as either flips for young buyers or student-friendly rentals.

BRRRR and long-term rental strategies fit areas like Garfield Park, Roosevelt Park, Baxter and parts of the southeast side, where purchase prices are lower and rental demand stays strong. Those neighborhoods also have more lead and code issues, so the scope must be thorough. Small multifamily properties, including duplexes and converted Victorians in Heritage Hill and Eastown, can produce solid rents but often need major system work. Inner-ring suburbs like Wyoming and Kentwood offer newer post-war housing that tends to need less structural work.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits in Grand Rapids are handled through the city’s Development Center, which coordinates plan review and inspections. Rehab work that changes structure, adds or moves plumbing fixtures, replaces electrical panels or alters heating systems will need permits, and many cosmetic projects that open walls will too. Inspections are scheduled at rough-in and final stages, and permits must be closed before you sell or rent.

The city requires rental properties to be certified. Code Compliance inspects rental units and issues a certificate when the property meets the housing code, and the certificate expires on a set schedule, so every rental is reinspected periodically. Inspectors focus on safety items like smoke detectors, egress, handrails, electrical hazards, heating and deteriorated paint.

Grand Rapids also has local historic districts, including Heritage Hill and Cherry Hill, where exterior changes such as windows, doors, siding, porches and roofing materials need approval from the Historic Preservation Commission. Approval should be secured before work starts. Genstone’s field manager coordinates permits through the licensed local contractors and keeps inspection results in your project file.
climate: West Michigan winters are cold, long and snowy, with lake-effect bands off Lake Michigan that can drop heavy snow on Grand Rapids in short bursts. Snow loads, ice dams and frozen pipes are the main winter risks for a rehab, especially in a vacant house. Exterior work like masonry, foundation excavation, roofing and painting is best done between late spring and early fall. Spring thaw can bring high water: the Grand River flooded significantly in 2013, and smaller streams like Plaster Creek on the southeast side have caused localized flooding. Summers are warm and humid, and damp air condenses on cool stone and block basement walls, so moisture control below grade matters in the older neighborhoods. Sump pumps, dehumidifiers and good gutter drainage are worth budgeting into most scopes.

faqs.q: How competitive is it to find flips in Grand Rapids?
faqs.a: Very competitive for clean houses. Owner-occupant buyers are active, and they often win homes that only need cosmetic work. Investors tend to find opportunities in houses with deferred maintenance, foundation issues, outdated systems or converted layouts. Those properties can work well, but only if the repair estimate is accurate. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built for that situation, so you know the cost of the work before your offer goes in.

faqs.q: Do you work in Heritage Hill and other historic districts?
faqs.a: Yes. Historic district work requires approval from the Historic Preservation Commission for many exterior changes, and the materials and methods must fit the character of the house. We include that review in the schedule and choose materials that the commission typically accepts. Interior work is usually less restricted, but large Victorian homes still need careful planning for wiring, plumbing and fire safety.

faqs.q: Can you help me pass the Grand Rapids rental certification inspection?
faqs.a: We build rental scopes around the items the city’s inspectors focus on, including smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, egress, handrails, electrical safety, heating and intact paint. That does not replace the city’s inspection, but it means the house is ready when the inspector arrives. If a unit fails, we can quickly address the items noted and help you schedule the reinspection.

faqs.q: Do you serve the suburbs around Grand Rapids?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates licensed local contractors throughout the Grand Rapids area, including Wyoming, Kentwood, Walker, Grandville and nearby communities. Each suburb has its own building department, and requirements for rentals and permits vary. We adjust the scope and permit plan to the town where the property is located, so the work fits local rules as well as your investment strategy.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Grand Rapids, MI | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Grand Rapids fix and flip contractor: pre-offer estimates on Eastown, Creston and Alger Heights homes, character-forward finishes and draws tied to progress.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Grand Rapids
fix-flip.intro: Grand Rapids buyers are picky in a specific way. They want the craftsmanship of an older house, such as quarter-sawn oak trim, leaded glass and built-in buffets, but they also want a kitchen that works, a bathroom that feels new and mechanical systems they will not have to replace. A flip that strips out the character in favor of generic finishes often sells slower than one that keeps it. Genstone Construction helps you plan that balance. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the repair cost and checks it against the comps your resale depends on. Once the house is yours, the scope lays out finish choices room by room, a single field manager runs the job, and the licensed local trades take out their permits through the city’s Development Center. You pay only as work is completed.

sections.h2: Flipping the old housing stock east of downtown
sections.body:
Eastown, East Hills and the edges of Heritage Hill are full of foursquares, Craftsman bungalows and smaller Victorians that sell well when they are renovated with care. Buyers here are often young professionals and families who chose an older neighborhood on purpose. They notice when original trim has been painted over, when a pocket door has been removed or when a stained glass window has been replaced with vinyl.

The rehab work in these houses tends to center on systems that were never fully updated. Knob-and-tube wiring may still be live in walls and ceilings. Supply lines are often galvanized, drains are cast iron and the furnace may be a converted gravity unit or a tired boiler. Balloon framing means fire blocking has to be added when walls are opened. Budgeting for full rewiring and repiping in these neighborhoods is usually more realistic than hoping to patch. Once the systems are handled, money spent on refinishing original floors and woodwork goes further with buyers than money spent on high-end fixtures.

sections.h2: Post-war flips in Alger Heights and Ottawa Hills
sections.body:
Farther south and east, Alger Heights and Ottawa Hills offer a different flip. Their brick Tudors, colonials and bungalows from the 1920s through the 1950s were built more consistently, with concrete block or poured basements, better framing and fewer conversions. Ottawa Hills has larger homes that attract higher-income buyers, while Alger Heights is a walkable neighborhood with smaller houses popular with first-time buyers.

In these houses, the scope tends to focus on updating kitchens and baths, refinishing floors, replacing windows that have failed and modernizing the electrical panel. Plaster walls are generally in better shape, and many homes have fireplaces and arched doorways buyers like. Basement finishing can add usable space, but only after moisture issues are handled. Before finishing a basement, we check for efflorescence, cracks and old water stains, and we look at the grading and gutters outside. A finished basement that leaks during the first spring thaw after closing is a costly problem for a flipper.

sections.h2: Controlling time and cost in a tight market
sections.body:
In a competitive market, the price you pay for a house leaves little margin for surprises. The most common budget problems in Grand Rapids flips are foundation water, hidden knob-and-tube wiring, roof and ice dam damage, and sewer lines with root intrusion or offset joints. Many of these can be found before purchase with a careful walk-through, a sewer camera and a close look at the attic and basement.

Our detailed scope lists each item with its labor and material cost, and the draw schedule shows when work will be paid. Your field manager coordinates trades so inspections happen on time and drywall does not go up before rough-ins are approved. If the house is in a historic district, we build Historic Preservation Commission review into the plan before exterior work starts. When hidden problems do appear, you get a documented change order with photos before work proceeds. That keeps carrying costs predictable and gives you a better chance of hitting the listing date you planned.

faqs.q: Should I keep original woodwork in a Grand Rapids flip?
faqs.a: In most of the older neighborhoods, yes, if it is in reasonable condition. Buyers in Eastown, East Hills and Heritage Hill often value original trim, built-ins and doors, and restoring them is frequently cheaper than replacing them with new millwork of similar quality. Painted-over woodwork can be stripped or simply repainted cleanly. We note salvageable features in the scope so they are protected during demolition.

faqs.q: Is finishing the basement worth it in a Grand Rapids flip?
faqs.a: It depends on the house and the comps. In Alger Heights and similar neighborhoods, finished basements can add appeal if they are dry and well done. In older homes with stone or rubble foundations, finishing is riskier because water control is harder. We look at the foundation, grading and comparable sales before recommending whether to finish the basement or keep it clean, dry and unfinished.

faqs.q: Do flips in Grand Rapids need permits for kitchen and bath remodels?
faqs.a: Usually. Moving or adding plumbing, adding electrical circuits, replacing panels or altering walls all trigger permits. Even a straightforward kitchen remodel often includes new circuits and plumbing connections. Closed permits matter at resale because buyers and their inspectors may ask. Each trade pulls its own permit through the city’s Development Center, and your field manager books the inspections and files the sign-offs.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Grand Rapids, MI | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR contractor in Grand Rapids: rehabs scoped for the refinance appraisal and city rental certification, with lead-safe work and durable rental finishes.
brrrr.h1: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Grand Rapids
brrrr.intro: The BRRRR method can work well in Grand Rapids because rents have held up and appraisers can find recent sales of renovated older homes. The challenge is buying low enough. Discounted properties here usually need significant work, and the rehab has to lift the value enough for a cash-out refinance while producing a rental that passes the city’s certification inspection. Genstone Construction scopes the work around both goals. Before you bid, the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tells you what the rehab will cost and whether the finished house is likely to support the loan you plan to refinance into. Then we build a scope that spends where appraisers and inspectors both look, using finishes that last through tenant turnover. Licensed local trades do the work under one field manager, and money moves only when a stage of the work is done.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods where the BRRRR math works
sections.body:
In Grand Rapids, the neighborhoods where you can buy below the post-rehab value tend to be on the southeast and west sides, along with parts of Creston. Garfield Park, Roosevelt Park, Baxter and the streets around John Ball Park all have older frame houses that rent well and sell to investors and first-time buyers. Purchase prices there leave room for a rehab, and rental demand is steady thanks to proximity to downtown, hospitals and the Grand Valley campus.

The trade-off is that these houses often have more deferred maintenance and more lead hazards than homes in Eastown or Alger Heights. Old windows, peeling exterior paint, outdated electrical systems and wet basements are common. For a BRRRR investor, that is not necessarily bad news. These are exactly the items that move an appraiser’s condition rating, and fixing them creates value. The key is estimating them accurately before you buy, so the refinance value covers both your purchase price and your full renovation budget.

sections.h2: Rehab items that matter to the appraiser
sections.body:
A Grand Rapids appraiser will line your house up against comparable sales and then adjust for condition, updates and features. A house with a new roof, updated electrical panel, newer furnace and water heater, refinished floors, updated kitchen and bath, and a dry basement will usually rate higher than one with fresh paint over old systems.

We help you focus the budget on items that change that rating. In many older homes, that means replacing knob-and-tube wiring, repiping galvanized supply lines, installing a high-efficiency furnace and fixing water entry in the basement. On the visible side, durable kitchen cabinets and counters, an updated bath with a tiled surround, new light fixtures and consistent flooring all help. We provide a detailed list of completed work with photos so you can give the appraiser a clear record of improvements. That documentation is especially useful when the house was in poor condition when you bought it, because it shows the transformation the appraiser needs to account for.

sections.h2: Passing rental certification and keeping tenants
sections.body:
Before you can rent, Grand Rapids requires the property to pass a rental certification inspection through Code Compliance. Inspectors check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, egress, handrails and guardrails, electrical hazards, heating, plumbing and the condition of painted surfaces. In older houses, deteriorated paint is a frequent issue and must be addressed with lead-safe work practices.

Those items go into the original rehab scope so the inspector sees finished work, not a list of corrections. That avoids failed inspections and delays to your first rent check, which matters because your refinance often depends on showing a lease or market rent. For long-term durability, we lean on waterproof plank flooring wherever water or snowmelt gets tracked in, semi-gloss paint on trim, solid-surface counters and standard fixtures that are easy to replace. Upgrading attic insulation and air sealing also helps tenants with winter heating costs, which reduces complaints and turnover in a city where January utility bills can be high.

faqs.q: Can I buy a Grand Rapids duplex for a BRRRR project?
faqs.a: Yes, and many investors do. Duplexes and converted older homes can produce strong rents, and appraisers may consider both the sales comparison and income approaches. These buildings often need more work on shared systems, such as roofs, foundations, plumbing stacks and electrical services. We scope both units and the shared items so you can see the full cost before you commit to the purchase.

faqs.q: How do lead requirements affect a BRRRR rehab in Grand Rapids?
faqs.a: Most rental houses in the city were built before 1978, so lead-based paint is likely. Federal rules require lead-safe work practices when paint is disturbed, and the city’s rental inspection checks for deteriorated paint. In practice, that means planning for window repairs or replacement, porch and trim stabilization and careful cleanup. Building these items into the scope prevents failed inspections and protects tenants.

faqs.q: Should I replace old windows in a BRRRR property?
faqs.a: Often, yes, especially if the windows are deteriorated, painted shut or have lead paint on friction surfaces. New windows reduce lead hazards, improve energy efficiency and can raise the appraiser’s condition rating. In historic districts, window replacement may require approval, and repairing original windows may be preferred. We price both repair and replacement so you can choose based on rent, value and local requirements.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Grand Rapids | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Grand Rapids rental renovation for single-family portfolios: certification-ready rehabs and turns, lead-safe practices and finishes that last through turnover.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovation in Grand Rapids
rental-renovation.intro: Owning single-family rentals in Grand Rapids means working with older housing, a rental certification program with regular inspections, and tenants who expect a warm, dry, safe home through a long West Michigan winter. Genstone Construction renovates and turns rental houses across the city and its suburbs. We help portfolio owners set a consistent standard for finishes and systems, then apply it across properties so estimates are predictable and turns are faster. Every house gets its own written scope and estimate, one field manager and licensed local trades who already work to the city’s inspection checklist. Between leases, Genstone Field Services can inspect, maintain, turn and correct code items so each house stays rentable without you supervising it.

sections.h2: A rental standard for older Grand Rapids homes
sections.body:
Grand Rapids rental portfolios often include houses from very different eras: a Victorian on the West Side, a 1920s bungalow in Garfield Park, a post-war ranch in Wyoming. A good standard accounts for those differences while keeping materials and finishes consistent where it makes sense.

For most properties, that includes luxury vinyl plank flooring in kitchens, baths and basements, durable carpet or refinished hardwood in bedrooms, neutral paint with semi-gloss trim, standard appliance packages and simple fixtures that your property manager can replace quickly. On the mechanical side, it means high-efficiency furnaces, updated electrical panels, GFCI protection where required and modern water heaters. In older houses, it also includes lead-safe window treatments and stabilized exterior paint. A shared standard lets the local contractors work faster because they know what to install, and it makes your maintenance costs easier to predict across the portfolio. We document the standard in your project files so future turns follow the same specifications.

Rental certification in Grand Rapids is not a one-time event, because Code Compliance comes back to reinspect when each certificate runs out. Every inspection is an opportunity for a property to fail on a missing smoke detector, a loose handrail, a cracked window or peeling paint. For a portfolio owner, those failures add up in time and reinspection costs.

We help by building certification requirements into every renovation and turn. Before a unit is rented again, we check the same items the city looks at: life safety devices, egress, stairs and rails, electrical safety, heat, plumbing and paint condition. In older houses, deteriorated paint gets attention with lead-safe practices because it is one of the most common failure points. Keeping consistent records of what was checked and repaired also helps when the next inspection comes due. Your property manager can pull a file for each address and see what was installed and when, which makes scheduling and preparation simpler.

sections.h2: Turns, winter prep and keeping vacancy short
sections.body:
Every week a rental sits empty costs you rent. In Grand Rapids, turnover usually includes cleaning, paint touch-ups, flooring repairs, appliance checks and repairs from tenant damage. Because the materials are already decided, a turn can be priced from the walk-through photos and crews can start shortly after move-out.

Winter adds risk. A vacant rental can freeze quickly during a lake-effect cold snap if the heat fails or is turned off, splitting pipes and damaging fixtures. If a unit will be vacant in the colder months, we recommend keeping heat on at a safe setting or winterizing the plumbing. Fall is also the time to check furnaces, clear gutters, extend downspouts and test sump pumps, particularly under the older houses where the basement walls are stone or block. Ice dams on poorly insulated roofs can cause interior water damage, so attic insulation and air sealing are worth considering during turns. Preventing water damage is usually far cheaper than repairing it after the fact.

faqs.q: Can Genstone handle make-ready work on my Grand Rapids rentals between tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. Turns and make-ready work are a core part of Genstone Field Services, alongside property inspections and maintenance in occupied homes. When a lease ends, we walk the unit, price the work against your portfolio standard and line it up with the next certification visit from Code Compliance. Your property manager receives photos of the finished unit and a list of what was replaced, so you can sign off on a turn in Roosevelt Park or Creston without driving over to look at it.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals in Wyoming, Kentwood and Walker as well?
faqs.a: Yes. Our network of licensed contractors covers Grand Rapids and the surrounding suburbs. Keep in mind that each of those cities runs its own building department and sets its own rules for rental housing, so the permit plan changes with the address. Suburban rentals are frequently 1950s and 1960s ranches with poured or block basements and fewer layers of old paint, which usually means fewer structural surprises than a West Side house from the 1890s.

faqs.q: Does the workmanship warranty cover damage a tenant causes?
faqs.a: No. The one-year warranty applies to defects in the work Genstone’s contractors performed, such as a leaking drain connection or a door that was hung out of plumb. Holes in drywall, broken blinds, pet damage to flooring and ordinary wear from years of occupancy fall outside it. That distinction is why our Grand Rapids rental scopes lean on hard-wearing materials, and why we photograph a unit at handover so you have a baseline if a deposit dispute comes up later.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Grand Rapids
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Grand Rapids duplex and 2–4 unit renovation: converted Victorians in Heritage Hill and Eastown, fire separation, split utilities and work around tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Grand Rapids
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily in Grand Rapids mostly means converted houses. During the middle of the last century, many large Victorians in Heritage Hill and Eastown, along with bigger homes on the West Side and southeast side, were divided into two, three or four apartments. You will also find purpose-built duplexes and small walk-ups scattered through older neighborhoods. These buildings can produce strong rents, but conversions done decades ago often left behind tangled wiring, shared plumbing, weak fire separation and awkward egress. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit buildings with those issues in mind. We plan around shared systems and occupied units, prepare a detailed scope and estimate, assign a field manager and coordinate licensed local contractors who pull permits through the city’s Development Center.

sections.h2: What to expect in a converted Grand Rapids Victorian
sections.body:
Converted Victorians are common in Heritage Hill, Eastown and nearby streets. They often have a unit on each floor, sometimes with a third unit in the attic. Kitchens were added where bedrooms or pantries used to be, bathrooms were squeezed into closets and new stairs were built to reach upper units. The work was usually done long before modern codes and often without much regard to fire separation or electrical capacity.

When you buy one, look closely at the electrical service and panels, the number of circuits serving each unit, the plumbing stacks and drain lines, and the separation between units. Egress from upper units should be clear and safe. Many buildings have exterior fire escapes or rear stairs that need repair or replacement. Heat may come from a shared boiler or from several furnaces installed at different times. In Heritage Hill, exterior changes also require Historic Preservation Commission approval. Our pre-offer review focuses on these shared and structural issues first because they drive the budget.

sections.h2: Fire separation, egress and shared systems
sections.body:
Safety is the biggest concern in older multi-unit conversions. Fire separation between units may be missing or compromised by open chases, unsealed penetrations and old doors that do not close properly. Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms may be missing or poorly located. Upper units sometimes rely on a single interior stair, which is a serious risk if it fills with smoke.

Correcting these issues often involves adding fire-rated drywall, sealing penetrations, installing self-closing doors, upgrading alarms and improving egress. Electrical services may need to be upgraded and split so each unit has its own meter and panel. Separate furnaces and water heaters can let tenants pay their own utilities, which reduces your operating costs. All of this work requires permits and inspections. We map out a plan for the whole building, including where equipment will go and how ducts and circuits will reach each unit, so you know the scope before you commit.

Many small multifamily buildings in Grand Rapids are purchased with some units occupied. Renovating a vacant unit while tenants live in others requires coordination. Contractors must work during reasonable hours, protect shared hallways and stairs, and give notice before shutting off water, heat or power.

Lead-safe practices are especially important in multi-unit buildings, because dust can spread through shared spaces and ductwork. We usually schedule shared system work, such as roof replacement, sewer repairs, electrical service upgrades and boiler replacement, in short, planned windows with advance notice. Interior work in vacant units can then proceed on a normal schedule. If an occupied unit needs repairs, we coordinate with your property manager or wait until the tenant moves out. This phased approach keeps rent coming in while the building improves and reduces conflict with tenants. It also helps you meet the city’s rental certification requirements for each unit as it comes online.

faqs.q: Could a converted Heritage Hill house go back to single-family?
faqs.a: In some cases it is the stronger exit. Buyers shopping Heritage Hill often want an intact Victorian, and a carefully restored house can draw a different pool than a three-unit rental. The path involves zoning confirmation, building permits, taking out added kitchens, reworking stairs and, for exterior changes, Historic Preservation Commission approval. We can price the building both ways so you can weigh a restoration sale against holding it for rent.

faqs.q: Does every apartment in the building have to pass the city’s rental inspection?
faqs.a: Yes. Code Compliance certifies each rental unit, and common areas such as the front hall, the rear stair and the shared basement are inspected along with the apartments. In older Grand Rapids conversions, the items that fail most often are missing alarms, poor separation between units, loose rails and deteriorated paint. We schedule the work so each unit is ready to be inspected as soon as it is finished rather than holding the whole building until the end.

faqs.q: Is splitting the heat and electric worth the cost in a converted house?
faqs.a: When an owner is paying for a single boiler that heats three apartments through a Grand Rapids winter, separating the systems often pays for itself in operating savings and fewer comfort complaints. The work is not small. It can mean new furnaces, duct runs threaded through plaster walls, additional gas piping and a service upgrade so Consumers Energy can set separate meters. We lay out the equipment locations and cost so you can compare that against adjusting rents to include heat.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Grand Rapids, MI | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Grand Rapids: itemized bids, HUD consultant coordination and draw records for buyers taking on older West Michigan homes.
fha-203k.h1: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor in Grand Rapids
fha-203k.intro: Ask a Grand Rapids listing agent what happens to a clean, updated three-bedroom on the West Side and the answer is usually a busy weekend of showings and several offers. The houses that linger are the ones with a dated kitchen, a furnace near the end of its life or a damp fieldstone basement. For buyers using FHA financing, those are exactly the houses where the 203(k) program pays off, because the purchase and the repairs are combined into one loan and the buyer is no longer competing on condition. Genstone Construction is a certified FHA 203(k) contractor. We prepare the itemized bid, work alongside the HUD consultant on Standard loans and document each draw for the lender. Licensed local contractors perform the work under Development Center permits, and one field manager stays on the file from the first walk-through to the final inspection.

sections.body:
The program works best on a house that is fundamentally sound but has fallen behind. In Grand Rapids, that describes a lot of Creston foursquares, Garfield Park and Alger Heights bungalows with original kitchens, and compact West Side cottages near John Ball Park that still run on old wiring. These homes tend to appraise well once updated because buyers already shop those streets.

The larger Victorians in Heritage Hill and Eastown can qualify too, but they need a sharper pencil. Slate or multi-layer roofs, stone foundations and many coats of old paint on elaborate trim can push the repair total higher than the finished value supports. Any exterior change in a local historic district also needs Historic Preservation Commission review, which belongs in the schedule.

Because FHA financing can be used on buildings of up to four units when the buyer lives in one of them, a converted house in Eastown can be a 203(k) candidate as well. Those deals usually involve fire separation and egress work, so they almost always fall under the Standard program.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard for an older West Michigan house
sections.body:
Lenders will want to know early which version of the loan fits, and the answer comes down to what kind of work the house needs. The Limited 203(k) handles non-structural repairs with a cap of $75,000. A typical Grand Rapids Limited job might replace windows with peeling lead paint, install a new furnace and water heater, replace an aging roof without structural repair, update the kitchen and bathroom and refinish the oak floors.

The Standard 203(k) carries a $5,000 minimum and requires a HUD-approved consultant to write up the work and inspect draws. It is the right tool when the scope includes structural items, such as rebuilding a bowing rubble foundation wall, reframing a sagging rear porch, removing a bearing wall to open a kitchen or adding a second bathroom. Program rules also change at the $15,000 inspection threshold. Our scope separates structural and cosmetic items line by line, which lets the buyer, agent and loan officer agree on the right path before an appraisal is ordered.

sections.h2: How the paperwork moves from bid to final draw
sections.body:
A 203(k) file lives or dies on the contractor bid. Ours lists every repair as its own item with its labor, material and permit cost shown separately, written so the appraiser can value the finished house and the consultant can match it to the work write-up. When the consultant’s write-up and our bid disagree, we reconcile them before closing rather than during construction.

After the loan closes, repair money sits in escrow and is released as stages are finished. Our field manager requests each draw with photos, confirms the matching Development Center inspection has passed, and gathers lien waivers from the trades before the lender releases funds. Grand Rapids weather affects the order of work, so we plan roofing, exterior paint and masonry for the warmer months and keep interior trades moving when lake-effect snow arrives. If hidden damage turns up, such as rotted sill plates behind old siding, the change order goes to the lender and consultant with photos before anyone touches it.

faqs.q: Can I buy a Grand Rapids duplex with a 203(k) loan?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as you will live in one of the units. FHA allows the 203(k) on properties with up to four units for an owner-occupant, and Grand Rapids has plenty of converted houses and side-by-side duplexes that fit. The renovation budget usually needs to cover shared items such as the roof, the electrical service and fire separation between units, so we price those first and then the interiors of each apartment.

faqs.q: Will sellers in Grand Rapids take a 203(k) offer seriously?
faqs.a: Many will, particularly on houses that have already scared off conventional buyers. What helps is showing the seller that the renovation plan is real. When we walk the house early and provide a preliminary scope, your agent can include it with the offer and explain the timeline. On a house with an old furnace, a wet basement and a dated kitchen, a prepared 203(k) buyer often looks more reliable than one who has not priced the work.

faqs.q: How does lead paint affect a 203(k) in an older Grand Rapids house?
faqs.a: FHA requires deteriorated paint in homes built before 1978 to be corrected, and nearly every house in the older Grand Rapids neighborhoods falls into that group. In practice, the scope will include paint stabilization or window replacement, attention to porch floors and exterior trim, and lead-safe work practices during the job. We include those items from the start so they do not surface as a surprise condition during the appraisal or the consultant’s inspection.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Grand Rapids, MI | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Grand Rapids REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: ice dam, sump and freeze damage repaired to financeable condition with line-item photo records.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Grand Rapids
reo-renovation.intro: Buyers absorb well-presented homes quickly in Grand Rapids, so a bank-owned property that is repaired to a financeable standard tends to move. The obstacle is the condition the house is in when the servicer finally gets the keys. A winter or two of vacancy in West Michigan can mean ice-dammed ceilings, a failed sump pump under a stone foundation, frozen supply lines and peeling paint that blocks FHA financing. Genstone Construction renovates REO homes in the city and surrounding suburbs on behalf of loan servicers, banks, REITs and funds, and holds preferred-contractor status with the Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Our estimators write line-item bids with photos, a field manager runs each property, and licensed local contractors work under city permits. Genstone Field Services can take on securing, winterization and recurring inspections so the house does not slide backward while bids are reviewed.

sections.h2: How vacancy shows up in Grand Rapids houses
sections.body:
The damage pattern in vacant Grand Rapids homes follows the seasons. Heavy lake-effect snow sits on roofs that nobody is clearing, and in older houses with little attic insulation the eaves form ice dams that push meltwater under the shingles and into plaster ceilings. When the power is cut or the furnace fails, water left in the lines freezes and splits them, and a house where the curb stop was never closed can flood from the first floor down.

Spring brings a second round. Stone and rubble foundations on the West Side and in Creston take on water during thaw, and a sump pump with no power or a seized float lets the basement fill. Low-lying streets near Plaster Creek on the southeast side are particularly prone. Raccoons and squirrels move into the attics of big Victorians through gaps around the eaves. Our first visit documents each of these conditions with photos, so the bid matches the house the asset manager now owns.

sections.h2: Repairing to a standard Grand Rapids buyers can finance
sections.body:
Most buyers for a renovated Grand Rapids house will be using FHA or conventional financing, and their appraiser will flag conditions that make the home ineligible. Missing or inoperable heat, a roof with active leaks, deteriorated paint on a pre-1978 house, exposed wiring and missing handrails are common reasons a sale stalls. We scope REO repairs to clear those items, because a property that can only sell to cash buyers usually sells for less.

Investor buyers bring a different checklist. If the next owner plans to rent, the house must pass the city’s rental certification through Code Compliance, which looks closely at alarms, egress, heating, electrical hazards and paint condition. Neglected properties may also carry open code cases for debris, overgrown yards or open structures. We review what is available on the property’s history and build the corrective work into the bid. The local contractors pull permits through the Development Center, and the closed permits go into the project file for the listing agent.

sections.h2: Reporting built around how asset managers work
sections.body:
An asset manager reviewing a dozen properties needs to approve or adjust a bid quickly and defend that decision later. Each Genstone bid is organized line by line with labor, materials and debris removal shown separately, and each line carries its own photos. Trash-outs on Grand Rapids REO homes are often heavy after a long vacancy, so dumpster and disposal costs are already in the number rather than added later.

During the work, the field manager updates progress against the approved scope and submits any change order with photos and an explanation of what was found, such as rotted subfloor under a toilet that only appeared once the vinyl came up. Lien waivers are collected as contractors are paid. Because Field Services is part of the same company, lawn care, re-securing, utility coordination and periodic inspections stay on one schedule with the renovation, which means the asset manager has one contact for the property from takeover through listing.

faqs.q: What should happen first when a Grand Rapids REO is taken over in winter?
faqs.a: Stop the freeze damage. That means confirming the water is off at the curb, draining and winterizing the system, and checking that the sump pump has power before the thaw. Genstone Field Services can handle the winterization, securing and an initial condition report while the asset manager reviews options. If the renovation will run through the cold months, we usually restore heat early so interior trades can work and drywall compound can cure.

faqs.q: Do you renovate REO properties for GSEs and servicers in Kent County?
faqs.a: Yes. Our client list for REO work spans the GSEs, which have named Genstone a preferred contractor, plus servicers, lenders, REITs and investment funds. In Grand Rapids and the nearby suburbs, we follow the client’s bid template and photo requirements, and we include notes on permit status and open code issues so the asset manager can see what stands between the property and a clean sale.

faqs.q: How much should we repair before listing a Grand Rapids REO?
faqs.a: That depends on the buyer pool you want. Repairing heat, roof leaks, electrical hazards, handrails and deteriorated paint usually opens the home to FHA and conventional buyers, who are plentiful in this market. Cosmetic upgrades beyond that may or may not return their cost. We can price a financeable-condition scope and a fuller renovation side by side so the asset manager can compare them against the broker’s pricing.
